title: Real-Time Volumetric Light Scattering
subtitle: Screen-Space God Rays in WebGL
excerpt: Implementing efficient screen-space volumetric light scattering using radial blur post-processing, inspired by GPU Gems 3 techniques.

sections.content: Volumetric lighting, often called "god rays" or crepuscular rays, adds dramatic atmosphere to any scene. While true volumetric rendering via raymarching is expensive, we can achieve convincing results using a clever screen-space approximation.

The technique works by performing radial blur sampling from the light source position in screen space. Each pixel samples along a ray toward the light, accumulating color and applying exponential decay.

sections.title: Fragment Shader - Radial Blur Pass

items: Render at half or quarter resolution for mobile
Use 64-128 samples for quality vs 32 for performance
Apply bilateral upscaling to preserve edges
Cache light screen position to avoid matrix multiplications per-fragment

sections.alt: Before and after volumetric lighting comparison
sections.caption: Left: Scene without god rays. Right: With screen-space volumetric scattering.

sections.content: The effect integrates as a post-process pass after your main scene render. First render an occlusion mask (dark silhouettes against bright sky), then apply the radial blur, finally composite additively with your scene.
For multiple light sources, render each volumetric pass separately and blend. However, this scales linearly with light count - consider limiting to 1-2 key lights.

This technique runs at 60fps on mid-range mobile GPUs at 720p with 64 samples. The key insight is that volumetric scattering is primarily a low-frequency effect - aggressive resolution scaling has minimal visual impact while dramatically improving performance.
